newsitem.title: UK: Emerging debt powers to all-time high in London.
newsitem.headline: Emerging debt powers to all-time high in London.

text.p: Hectic trading pushed a euphoric emerging debt market to an all time-high in London, with prices advancing along a dual front headed by Russia and Mexico.
"The market has reached an all-time record high," said Ousmene Mandeng, fixed income strategist at West Merchant Bank. "It's topped the highest level it reached in January 1994."
"Everything is continuing to move higher," added a trader at a US firm in London, adding news from Russia and Mexico were driving the activity.

The most heavily traded Russian instruments -- dollar Vnesh loans RUVNUSLNS and the Min Fin 4 RU3E03=RR, were both up 1/2 a point. Dollar Vnesh climbed to 71-00 bid side, while the Min Fin 4 was bid at 52-1/2.

"Today the catalyst is the pricing of the Mexican Eurobond," the trader said. The $750 million 20-year deal, launched on Monday, is due to be priced between 450 and 462.5 basis points over Treasurieslater this week.
Traders says it expected to attract good buying interest that may steepen the yield curve for Mexican debt.
An outstanding long-dated Mexican bond, due in 2026, is trading at 470 b.p. over and is looking expensive in comparison, Mandeng said.
"We're seeing strong demand for other Latins off the back of it," the trader added.
Brazilian C bonds BR8D14=RR rose half a point to 70-00 while Argentine FRBs ARFLCO5=RR, one of the morning's best performers, climbed 7/8 to 84-1/2.

But Russian debt continued to go from strength to strength. Market talk that the country's planned Eurobond issue, expected in November, may come as early as the end of October, and optimism that its projected debt rating would be announced earlier than hoped, drove eastern European debt prices steadily upwards during the morning session.

Traders are confident that there are no hitches left in the country's debt rescheduling agreement with commercial banks, after the government announced last week that it had passed the amount of commitments from creditors which it needs for the deal to go ahead.
"At these price levels completion of the deal is priced in. There is no probability of failure at these levels," said one trader in Vnesh debt at a European bank in London.
Mandeng said that some players even held hopes that the rating agencies may even deliver an investment grade cachet rather than the BB level generally expected.
Even Bulgaria, the year's worst performer and which has been ostracised lately for dragging its feet on implementing IMF-requested reforms, shook off its lethargy during the morning.
FLIRBs BGFLIRB=RR climbed a full point to 30-00 after news yesterday that Sofia was starting to close down some of the country's loss-making banks, and that reserves were up slightly in August.

Investors fear the country may default on its Brady bonds if it does not receive crucial IMF funds which will only be released once Sofia has fulfilled the Fund's requirements. --Caroline Brothers, London Newsroom +44 171 542 2734
